Rite of Passage. A ritualized ceremony or series of ceremonies through which individuals transition between defined social statuses, from childhood to adulthood, from unmarried to married, or from living to ancestor status.

These ceremonial practices exist across human cultures and historical periods, marking moments when an individual's relationship to community, responsibilities, and identity fundamentally shift. Rites of passage typically involve three phases. Separation removes the person from normal society. Liminality places them in a threshold state outside normal categories. Reintegration incorporates them into their new status.

The Maasai of East Africa are renowned for elaborate age-set ceremonies through which boys undergo tests and initiation to become warriors, demonstrating strength and cultural knowledge. Across cultures, puberty rituals universally mark the transition to adult status, though specific practices vary dramatically, from scarification to seclusion to intellectual trials. Some rites involve ordeals or suffering, which anthropologists interpret as both testing worthiness and creating visceral memory that cements transformation and group loyalty.

Rites of passage often coincide with acquiring new knowledge, responsibilities, or privileges. These include rights to marry, inherit, participate in rituals, or hold status. Many modern Western societies lack institutionalized rites of passage, leading some scholars to argue that adolescence itself becomes prolonged and identity uncertain without ceremonial markers.
